summary.one_sentence: ClawBench evaluates browser agents on 153 write-heavy everyday tasks across 144 live production websites while intercepting the terminal request and retaining five synchronized evidence layers for scoring.
summary.thesis: A realistic web-agent benchmark can preserve live-site dynamics without committing the intended irreversible action if each task defines a terminal HTTP request to intercept and each verdict is grounded in a human reference plus a multi-layer execution trace.
summary.why_it_matters: It treats browser-agent evaluation as an infrastructure problem spanning isolation, effect control, recording, reference collection, and outcome verification rather than as action prediction over static pages.

prior_state: Static-trace web benchmarks evaluate action prediction over recorded pages rather than end-to-end task execution.
Self-hosted web environments improve reproducibility but omit production-site drift, authentication flows, anti-automation systems, and platform-specific validation.
Earlier live-web benchmarks primarily emphasize read-only information retrieval instead of purchases, reservations, applications, and detailed form submissions.
Executing write-heavy tasks on production services risks creating orders, messages, reservations, or other irreversible side effects.
URL, final-page, screenshot, or reference-action matching can miss alternative valid paths and does not expose enough evidence for auditing consequential workflows.
problem.key_gap: The missing capability is a safe, auditable way to measure whether an agent can complete heterogeneous, state-changing daily web workflows on production websites.
assumptions: A task's irreversible effect can be bounded by one annotated terminal HTTP request.
Human annotators can produce a valid reference trajectory and terminal payload for each retained task.
Five synchronized trace layers contain enough evidence for a judge to compare outcomes even when the agent follows a different path.
A shared browser harness and fresh per-run container make cross-model comparisons meaningful at the model-plus-harness level.
Website owners' policies and low-volume responsible use remain constraints even when the final request is blocked.

concepts.name: Daily-life task card
concepts.definition: An auditable task specification containing the instruction, starting URL, required user files or profile fields, expected final state, and terminal submission target.

concepts.name: Final-request interception
concepts.definition: A task-scoped mechanism that captures and blocks the annotated terminal HTTP request before it reaches the production server.

concepts.name: Five-layer trace
concepts.definition: Synchronized session video, action screenshots, HTTP traffic, agent messages, and browser actions recorded for evaluation and diagnosis.

concepts.name: Human reference trajectory
concepts.definition: A human execution of the same task under the same recording setup, including the expected terminal request and payload.

concepts.name: Agent-as-Judge
concepts.definition: A fixed-prompt evaluator that compares the task instruction, constraints, human reference, agent trace, and intercepted payload to produce a binary verdict with evidence-grounded justification.

concepts.name: Task-scoped safety envelope
concepts.definition: The bounded guarantee provided by intercepting an audited terminal endpoint; it is explicitly not a guarantee that arbitrary browsing is side-effect-free.

method.core_idea: Collect broad everyday write-heavy tasks, have a human complete each task to identify the terminal committing request, run every model-task pair in a fresh instrumented browser container, block the matching terminal request at runtime, and score the retained agent trace against the human reference with a fixed Agent-as-Judge protocol.
action_grammar: task card: instruction, starting URL, user data, expected final state, and terminal request schema.
observation: accessibility tree, DOM snapshot, or screenshot exposed through the browser harness.
action: navigate, click, type, scroll, observe, take_screenshot, or wait.
terminal request: URL pattern, HTTP method, and required payload fields that would commit the task.
interception event: captured terminal payload plus a blocked outbound request.
trajectory: synchronized session video, screenshots, HTTP traffic, agent messages, and browser actions.
reference: human trajectory and intercepted payload recorded under the same setup.
verdict: binary pass/fail with a structured, evidence-grounded justification.
metric: mean task-level success rate over the selected task set.
steps: Gather realistic write-heavy tasks from everyday website use and filter out read-only, unavailable, geographically restricted, paid, hard-verification, or unbounded-side-effect workflows.
Formalize each retained task as a task card with required personal data, expected final state, and a terminal submission target.
Record a human reference run and annotate the terminal request's URL pattern, method, and required payload fields.
Launch each model-task pair in a fresh isolated container with a clean Chromium profile, fixed resources, shared task data, and common browser actions.
Let the agent interact with the live production website while the extension and CDP sidecar record browser and network activity.
Capture and block the annotated terminal request before it reaches the server; leave ordinary page, image, analytics, and other non-terminal traffic intact.
Assemble the five-layer trace and compare it with the human reference and terminal payload through the fixed Agent-as-Judge prompt.
Aggregate binary verdicts into overall and category-level success rates, then use the recorded traces for failure diagnosis.
method.pseudocode:
task = load_task_card(task_id)
reference = load_human_reference(task_id)
run = start_fresh_container(model, task)

while run.active and within_limits:
    observation = run.browser.observe()
    action = agent.act(task.instruction, observation, run.history)
    request = run.browser.execute(action)
    run.trace.record(observation, action, request)
    if matches_terminal_schema(request, task.eval_schema):
        payload = capture(request)
        block(request)
        break

verdict = judge(task, reference, run.trace, payload)
success_rate = mean(verdict == PASS for each task)

claims.statement: The paper's benchmark contains 153 everyday tasks spanning 144 live production websites and 15 fine-grained life and work categories.
caveats: The breadth-first design emphasizes cross-site generalization rather than dense coverage within each domain.

claims.statement: ClawBench evaluates write-heavy, state-changing workflows on live production websites rather than action prediction on static traces or interaction only in self-hosted replicas.
caveats: Live sites improve ecological validity but change over time and prevent exact rerun determinism.

claims.statement: The final-request interceptor captured and blocked every annotated terminal request reached in the 153 human reference runs, with zero false-positive blocks on recorded navigation traffic.
caveats: This audit supports only the annotated terminal endpoints; it does not make arbitrary browsing side-effect-free.

claims.statement: Every run is recorded as five synchronized evidence layers and judged against a human reference trajectory with an outcome-oriented binary protocol.
caveats: Binary outcome scoring abstracts away partial progress and depends on the quality of the reference and judge prompt.

claims.statement: On the reported human-adjudicated comparisons, Agent-as-Judge agreement is 93.46% for Claude Sonnet 4.6 trajectories and 84.97% for GPT-5.4 trajectories.
caveats: Agreement is not perfect, and Claude Sonnet 4.6 shares a model family with the judge.

claims.statement: Across the shared eight-model evaluation, the highest overall success rate is 33.3%, and 68 of 153 tasks are solved by none of the evaluated models.
caveats: These are paper-era results for specific models under one shared OpenClaw harness, prompt, browser configuration, and action interface.

claims.statement: Each model-task pair runs in a fresh isolated container with a clean Chromium profile, fixed resource limits, a 30-minute wall-clock cap, and a five-minute idle watchdog.
caveats: Isolation controls shared state and resources but does not remove live-site drift or provider-side variability.

evidence.result: The paper reports 153 tasks across 144 live production websites, organized into 8 high-level groups and 15 fine-grained categories.

Tasks involve purchases, reservations, applications, account updates, and detailed form submissions on production websites, carrying user-specific data through platform validation toward a state-changing action.
The interceptor blocked every annotated terminal request reached in the 153 human reference runs and produced zero false-positive blocks on recorded navigation traffic.
evidence.metric: terminal-request coverage and navigation false positives

evidence.result: The five-layer trace is session video, action screenshots, HTTP traffic, agent messages, and browser actions; Agent-as-Judge compares it with the human reference and intercepted payload to return a binary verdict and justification.
Raw agreement with human verdicts is 93.46% for Claude Sonnet 4.6 and 84.97% for GPT-5.4 over the reported 153-task comparisons.
Claude Sonnet 4.6 scores 33.3%, Qwen 3.5 scores 26.1%, and GLM-5 scores 24.2%; 68 of 153 tasks are solved by no model and no task is solved by all eight.
evidence.metric: task success rate and task-level saturation

evidence.result: Each run uses an isolated container and fresh Chromium profile with 16 GB RAM, 8 vCPU, 32 GB disk, a 1,800-second wall-clock limit, and a five-minute idle timeout.

agent_infra_takeaways: A browser-agent benchmark measures a model-plus-harness system; the harness, prompt, browser configuration, and action interface must be held constant for comparative claims.
Effect control is strongest at a narrow, machine-checkable boundary: the terminal network request is easier to audit and block than an agent's stated intention.
The safety envelope is task-scoped. Workflows with multiple irreversible intermediate effects should be excluded rather than treated as covered.
Auditability requires synchronized evidence from the UI, network, agent transcript, low-level actions, and full-session replay.
Human references remain useful when they specify the target state and field bindings without forcing the agent to copy one exact action sequence.
Fresh browser profiles and isolated containers reduce cross-run leakage, but production-site and provider drift still need to be recorded and reported.
Binary success should be paired with trace-level diagnostics so last-mile hesitation, anti-bot blocking, early exit, and malformed submissions remain visible.
caveats: Live production websites trade rerun determinism for ecological validity; layouts, A/B tests, region, account state, and anti-automation systems can change.
Final-request interception is not a general browser sandbox and only covers the audited terminal endpoint for each task.
Live sessions, model calls, network instrumentation, and trace-based judging make repeated trials and ablations more expensive than static benchmarks.
Reported model scores are conditioned on the shared OpenClaw harness and should not be read as model-only capability measurements.
Agent-as-Judge uses a binary pass/fail metric that compresses intermediate progress and retains non-zero disagreement with human reviewers.
Claude Sonnet 4.6 shares a model family with the judge, creating a potential evaluator-family effect despite the reported human audit.
The breadth-first suite underrepresents mobile-only, non-English, and accessibility-dependent workflows.
The paper's model results are a dated snapshot; later models, harnesses, site states, or benchmark versions can change the ranking.

related_work.note: WebArena supplies reproducible self-hosted sites and functional validators; ClawBench instead accepts live-site variability to test production constraints and write-heavy tasks.

related_work.title: Mind2Web
related_work.note: Mind2Web evaluates web actions over recorded pages; ClawBench evaluates end-to-end execution and terminal effects on live sites.

related_work.note: OSWorld evaluates open-ended computer use in virtual machines; ClawBench focuses on broad everyday workflows across live web platforms.
